name: Carbon Footprint (Travel)
description: Estimates the carbon dioxide emissions of a trip by multiplying distance traveled by an emission factor per kilometer. The factor reflects the emissions of the chosen mode of transport.
notes: Distance in kilometers and factor in kg CO2 per km; result is kilograms of CO2. Accuracy depends entirely on choosing an emission factor that matches the actual vehicle and occupancy.

name: Gaussian Plume Dispersion
description: Computes the ground-level or receptor pollutant concentration downwind of a continuous point source using the Gaussian plume model, combining the emission rate, wind speed, lateral and vertical dispersion, and an image term for ground reflection.
notes: Assumes steady wind, flat terrain, and total ground reflection (the second exponential is the mirror source). Dispersion coefficients sy and sz grow with downwind distance and stability class; result is mass per volume.

name: Plume Rise (Holland)
description: Estimates the rise of a smokestack plume above the stack top using Holland's formula, (vs*d/u)*(1.5 + 0.00268*P*d*(Ts-Ta)/Ts), combining momentum from the exit velocity and buoyancy from the stack-to-ambient temperature difference.
notes: The first term is momentum rise and the second buoyancy rise; P is in hPa (mbar), temperatures in kelvin, lengths in metres. Empirical and best for neutral stability; add plume rise to physical stack height for effective height.

name: BOD Exerted (first order)
description: Gives the biochemical oxygen demand exerted after a given time using first-order decay, as the ultimate BOD times (1 minus 10 raised to the power -k*t). It represents the oxygen consumed by microbes up to time t.
notes: The rate constant k here is base-10 (per day), matching the 10^ form; convert if your k is base-e. Result approaches the ultimate BOD L0 as time increases and never exceeds it.

name: BOD by Dilution
description: Calculates biochemical oxygen demand from a dilution test as the drop in dissolved oxygen (initial minus final DO) divided by the dilution fraction of sample in the bottle. It scales the measured oxygen depletion back to the undiluted sample.
notes: The dilution fraction Pf is the volume of sample divided by total bottle volume (a value between 0 and 1). Valid tests require a measurable, non-excessive DO drop, typically leaving adequate residual oxygen.

name: Streeter-Phelps Oxygen Deficit
description: Predicts the dissolved-oxygen deficit in a river downstream of an organic load using the Streeter-Phelps model, balancing deoxygenation from BOD decay against reaeration over travel time t. It combines the BOD-driven deficit with the decaying initial deficit.
notes: Rates kd and kr must be in the same time units as t, and the term diverges if kr equals kd. Deficit is oxygen below saturation; the model assumes steady, plug-flow conditions with constant rate constants.

name: CO2 Equivalent (GWP)
description: Converts a mass of greenhouse gas into its carbon-dioxide equivalent by multiplying the gas mass by its global warming potential (GWP). This expresses the gas's climate impact on a common CO2 basis.
notes: GWP is dimensionless and tied to a specific time horizon (commonly 100 years), so use the value matching your reporting standard. Result units follow the input mass unit (here kg CO2e).

name: Carbon Footprint (Energy)
description: Estimates carbon dioxide emissions from energy use by multiplying energy consumed by an emission factor. It converts electricity or fuel energy into the associated mass of CO2 released.
notes: The emission factor depends on the energy source and grid mix (kg CO2 per kWh), so use a region- and year-specific value. Energy and factor units must be consistent (both per kWh).

name: Air Quality Index (linear)
description: Interpolates an Air Quality Index value for a measured pollutant concentration by linearly scaling between the index and concentration breakpoints of its category. The result is the AQI corresponding to concentration C.
notes: C must lie between the lower and upper concentration breakpoints of the correct pollutant category, and all concentrations must share units. Use the official breakpoint table for the specific pollutant.

name: Box Model Concentration
description: Estimates the steady-state pollutant concentration over an area using a box model: emission rate divided by the product of wind speed, box width, and mixing height. It assumes emissions are uniformly mixed in a ventilated box.
notes: Assumes steady state and complete vertical mixing up to the mixing height, with wind perpendicular to the box width. Keep units consistent (e.g. g/s, m/s, m) so the result comes out in g/m^3.

name: Gas Concentration ppmv to mg/m³ (25°C)
description: Converts a gas concentration from parts per million by volume to mass per volume (mg/m^3) at 25°C by multiplying ppmv by molecular weight and dividing by the molar volume 24.45 L/mol. It gives the mass concentration of the gas in air.
notes: The constant 24.45 L/mol is the molar volume of an ideal gas at 25°C and 1 atm; use a different molar volume for other temperatures or pressures. Molecular weight must be in g/mol.

name: Logistic Population Growth
description: Gives the population size at time t under logistic growth, which starts near-exponential and levels off at the carrying capacity Kc. It uses the initial population, growth rate, and elapsed time.
notes: The growth rate r must be in units matching time t (here per year); the model assumes constant carrying capacity and rate. Population rises toward but never exceeds Kc for N0 below Kc.

name: Surface Overflow Rate
description: Computes the surface overflow (loading) rate of a settling basin as the flow rate divided by the settling surface area. It equals the critical settling velocity of particles that are just fully removed.
notes: Flow and area units must be consistent so the result is a velocity (m/day). It reflects ideal sedimentation theory and does not account for turbulence, short-circuiting, or particle interactions.

name: Chick's Law Disinfection
description: Predicts the surviving microorganism count after disinfection using Chick's law of first-order inactivation: initial count times e to the power of negative inactivation rate times contact time. Longer contact reduces survivors exponentially.
notes: The rate constant k and contact time t must use matching time units (here per minute). Real disinfection often deviates from ideal first-order behavior due to shoulder or tailing effects.

name: Vehicle CO2 Emissions
description: Calculates the carbon dioxide emitted by a vehicle over a trip as distance times fuel consumption per distance times the fuel's emission factor. It gives total CO2 for the journey.
notes: Fuel consumption here is volume per distance (L/km), not the more common L/100km, so convert if needed. The emission factor is fuel-specific (kg CO2 per liter).

name: Bioconcentration Factor
description: Computes the bioconcentration factor, BCF = C_organism/C_water, the ratio of a pollutant's concentration in an aquatic organism's tissue to its concentration in the surrounding water at equilibrium.
notes: A high BCF flags substances (e.g. many lipophilic organics) that accumulate strongly in tissue relative to water. Assumes steady-state uptake from water only, ignoring dietary exposure routes.

name: Exponential Population Size
description: Projects population size under unlimited exponential growth, N0*exp(r*t), where r is the intrinsic per-capita growth rate and t the elapsed time. Population increases (or decreases if r<0) by a constant proportional rate.
notes: Assumes no resource limits, so it overestimates real populations over long times; a negative r gives exponential decline. Keep the units of r and t consistent (r is per unit time).

name: Logistic Population Size (Solution)
description: Gives the closed-form logistic growth curve, the population at time t under density-dependent growth toward carrying capacity K. Starting from N0 the population follows an S-shaped approach to K set by the growth rate r.
notes: The population asymptotes to K and never exceeds it when N0<K; if N0>K it declines toward K. Units of r and t must match, and K must be positive.

name: Discrete Population Growth (Geometric)
description: Projects population size for organisms with discrete, non-overlapping generations, N0*lambda^t, where lambda is the finite rate of increase per generation. The population multiplies by lambda each generation.
notes: lambda>1 means growth, lambda<1 decline, and lambda=1 a stable population; it relates to the continuous rate by lambda=e^r. t is counted in generations, not continuous time.

name: Intrinsic Rate of Increase (from R0)
description: Estimates the intrinsic rate of increase r from the net reproductive rate R0 and the generation time T, as ln(R0)/T. It approximates the continuous per-capita growth rate implied by lifetime reproduction.
notes: This is an approximation valid when growth is near stable; R0>1 gives positive r (growth), R0<1 negative. T should be the mean generation time in the same time units as the desired r.

name: Levins Metapopulation Equilibrium
description: Gives the equilibrium fraction of habitat patches occupied in Levins' metapopulation model, 1 - ex/co, where co is the colonization rate and ex the extinction rate. Persistence requires colonization to outpace extinction.
notes: The metapopulation persists only when co>ex, otherwise the equilibrium is at or below zero (regional extinction). Rates are per unit time and must share the same time units.

name: Instantaneous Growth Rate (from Counts)
description: Back-calculates the instantaneous per-capita growth rate r from two population counts separated by time t, as ln(Nt/N0)/t. It is the exponential growth rate that would carry N0 to Nt over that interval.
notes: Assumes exponential (density-independent) growth between the two counts; r is positive for growth, negative for decline. Nt and N0 must be positive and t expressed in the desired time units.

name: Lotka-Volterra Prey Equilibrium
description: Gives the equilibrium prey abundance in the classic Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model, gamma/delta, where gamma is the predator death rate and delta the efficiency of converting prey into predators. It is the prey level that keeps predator numbers steady.
notes: This equilibrium sets the predator's growth to zero, not the prey's; the idealized model assumes no prey carrying capacity. Rates gamma and delta must use consistent time units.

name: Lotka-Volterra Predator Equilibrium
description: Gives the equilibrium predator abundance in the Lotka-Volterra model, alpha/beta, where alpha is the prey's intrinsic growth rate and beta the predation rate coefficient. It is the predator level that holds prey numbers constant.
notes: This equilibrium makes the prey growth zero, not the predator's; the idealized model omits density dependence in the prey. Ensure alpha and beta use consistent units.

name: Two-Species Competition Equilibrium (N1)
description: Gives the equilibrium abundance of species 1 in the Lotka-Volterra competition model, (K1 - alpha*K2)/(1 - alpha*beta), where K1 and K2 are carrying capacities and alpha, beta the interspecific competition coefficients. It is the coexistence point for species 1.
notes: A stable, positive coexistence requires alpha*beta<1 and each species limiting itself more than the other; otherwise one species excludes the other. Competition coefficients convert individuals of one species into equivalents of the other.

name: Ricker Population Model
description: Projects next generation's population in the discrete Ricker model, Nt*exp(r*(1-Nt/K)), which combines geometric growth with density dependence relative to carrying capacity K. It is widely used for fish and insect stocks with overlapping density effects.
notes: High r values can produce oscillations or chaos rather than a smooth approach to K. Nt and K share the same population units, and the model advances one discrete generation per evaluation.

name: Beverton-Holt Recruitment Model
description: Gives next-generation recruitment in the Beverton-Holt model, R0*Nt/(1+Nt/M), a density-dependent stock-recruitment curve that saturates as population rises. R0 is the maximum per-capita growth at low density and M the half-saturation abundance.
notes: Unlike the Ricker model, recruitment rises monotonically to a plateau without overshoot or oscillation. Nt and M use the same population units; the plateau is R0*M individuals.

name: Theta-Logistic Growth Rate
description: Computes the instantaneous population growth rate under the theta-logistic model, r*N*(1-(N/K)^theta), which generalizes logistic growth by letting the shape parameter theta bend the density-dependence curve. It returns the rate of change of N, not the population itself.
notes: theta=1 recovers standard logistic growth; theta>1 concentrates density limitation near K, and theta<1 spreads it toward low densities. Growth is positive below K and negative above it.

name: Holling Type II Functional Response
description: Computes the number of prey a predator consumes over total time T at prey density N, a*T*N/(1+a*h*N), where a is the attack rate and h the handling time. Consumption rises with prey density but saturates because handling time limits intake.
notes: The response plateaus at T/h as prey become abundant, reflecting a maximum feeding rate. Attack rate and handling time must be consistent with the units of N and T.

name: Holling Type III Functional Response
description: Computes a sigmoidal (Type III) predator functional response, a*N^2/(1+a*h*N^2), where consumption scales with the square of prey density N. The S-shape produces low predation at scarce prey and saturation at high density.
notes: The accelerating low-density region can stabilize prey populations, unlike Type II. Here the response is per unit time; multiply by total time if a total consumption is needed.

name: Kleiber's Law (Metabolic Rate)
description: Estimates an organism's basal metabolic rate from body mass using Kleiber's law, B0*M^0.75, where B0 is a taxon-specific normalization constant and M the body mass in kilograms. Metabolic rate scales with the three-quarter power of mass.
notes: The 3/4 exponent means larger animals have lower metabolic rate per unit mass; B0 sets the units of the result. Empirical, so use it as an allometric approximation rather than an exact value.

name: Allometric Scaling Equation
description: Applies the general allometric power law a*M^b, relating a biological trait to body mass M through a scaling coefficient a and exponent b. It describes how physiological or morphological traits change disproportionately with size.
notes: b<1 means the trait grows slower than mass, b>1 faster, and b=1 in direct proportion; a fixes the units and value at unit mass. Fit a and b empirically from log-log regression.

name: Species-Area Relationship
description: Predicts the number of species expected in an area A using the power-law species-area relationship c*A^z, where c is a constant and z the scaling exponent. Species richness increases with area but with diminishing returns.
notes: z typically falls near 0.2-0.3 for islands; c depends on taxon, region, and area units. The relationship is empirical and best applied within the range of areas used to fit it.

name: Chapman Mark-Recapture Estimator
description: Estimates total population size from a mark-recapture study using the bias-corrected Chapman estimator, (M+1)*(C+1)/(R+1) - 1, where M were marked, C caught in the second sample, and R of those were marked recaptures. It corrects the simple Lincoln-Petersen index for small samples.
notes: Assumes a closed population, random mixing, and no mark loss between samples. The +1 corrections reduce bias and avoid division by zero when no marked animals are recaptured.

name: Gross Primary Productivity
description: Computes gross primary productivity as the sum of net primary productivity NPP and autotrophic respiration Rr. GPP is the total carbon fixed by producers before any is spent on their own respiration.
notes: NPP and Rr must be in the same units (here g/m² per year) for the sum to be meaningful. GPP always exceeds NPP because respiration Rr is positive.

name: Shannon Evenness (Pielou's J)
description: Computes Pielou's evenness J by dividing the observed Shannon diversity H by its maximum possible value ln(S) for S species. It measures how equally individuals are distributed among species, from 0 to 1.
notes: J=1 means perfectly even abundances and lower values indicate dominance by a few species. H must use natural logarithms to match ln(S), and S must be at least 2.

name: Inverse Simpson Index
description: Converts Simpson's index Ds (the probability that two randomly chosen individuals are the same species) into the inverse Simpson diversity 1/Ds. The result is an effective number of species, higher when the community is more diverse.
notes: Ds must be greater than 0 and at most 1; a community with all individuals in one species gives Ds=1 and diversity 1. This form weights common species and equals the Hill number of order 2.

name: Berger-Parker Dominance Index
description: Computes the Berger-Parker dominance index as Nmax/N, the abundance of the most common species divided by the total abundance. It gives the proportional dominance of the single most abundant species in the community.
notes: The index ranges from near 0 (no dominance) to 1 (one species only); higher values mean lower diversity. Its reciprocal is sometimes reported so that larger numbers indicate greater diversity.

name: Margalef's Richness Index
description: Computes Margalef's species richness index, (S-1)/ln(N), which adjusts the number of species S for sample size using the total number of individuals N. It allows richness comparison between samples of different sizes.
notes: N must exceed 1 so ln(N) is positive, and the index assumes larger samples naturally contain more species. It has no upper bound and is sensitive to sample size and sampling effort.

name: Menhinick's Richness Index
description: Computes Menhinick's richness index, S/sqrt(N), dividing the number of species S by the square root of the total number of individuals N. Like Margalef's index it standardizes species count against sample size.
notes: N must be positive; the square-root correction assumes richness grows with the root of abundance. The index remains sensitive to sampling effort and lacks a fixed upper bound.

name: Age-Specific Survivorship (lx)
description: Computes the survivorship lx of a life table as nx/n0, the fraction of the original cohort still alive at age x. It gives the probability that an individual survives from birth to age x.
notes: lx starts at 1 at age 0 and declines monotonically with age; nx cannot exceed n0. It reflects cumulative survival, not the survival within a single age interval.

name: Age-Specific Mortality Rate (qx)
description: Computes the age-specific mortality rate qx as dx/nx, the number dying during interval x divided by the number alive at its start. It is the probability of dying within that single age interval.
notes: qx lies between 0 and 1 and applies only to one interval, unlike cumulative survivorship. Deaths dx cannot exceed the survivors nx entering the interval.

name: Immigration Rate (Island Biogeography)
description: Gives the immigration rate of new species onto an island in MacArthur-Wilson theory, I0*(1-S/P), where I0 is the maximum rate, S the species already present, and P the mainland species pool. Immigration falls as the island fills up.
notes: The rate declines linearly to zero when S reaches the pool size P, since no new species remain to arrive. S should not exceed P, and rates share the same time units.

name: Extinction Rate (Island Biogeography)
description: Gives the extinction rate of species on an island in MacArthur-Wilson theory, E0*S/P, rising in proportion to the number of species present S relative to the pool P. More species mean more that can go locally extinct.
notes: The rate grows linearly with S and reaches its maximum E0 when the island holds the full pool. Rates use the same time units as immigration for the equilibrium comparison.

name: Equilibrium Species Richness (Island Biogeography)
description: Estimates the equilibrium number of species on an island where immigration balances extinction, I0*P/(I0+E0). It combines the maximum immigration rate I0, maximum extinction rate E0, and mainland pool P into the steady-state richness.
notes: This is a simplified linear-rate result; larger I0 relative to E0 pushes richness toward the full pool P. It predicts a dynamic equilibrium with ongoing species turnover.

name: Lindeman Ecological Efficiency
description: Computes trophic (ecological) efficiency as Pn/Pprev, the production at trophic level n divided by production at the level below it. It is the fraction of energy at one level that is passed up to the next.
notes: Values are typically around 0.1 (the ten-percent rule), and both productions must share the same energy units. Low efficiency is why food chains have few trophic levels.

name: Biomass Turnover Rate
description: Computes the biomass turnover rate as production Pr divided by standing biomass B. It expresses how many times the standing biomass is replaced per unit time, or equivalently the inverse of the biomass residence time.
notes: Production and biomass must use compatible units so the ratio comes out per unit time (here per year). A high turnover means rapidly replaced, short-lived biomass.

name: Whittaker's Beta Diversity
description: Computes Whittaker's beta diversity, beta = gamma/alpha - 1, the amount of species turnover between sites relative to the average within-site (alpha) richness and the total pooled (gamma) richness.
notes: A value of 0 means every site has the same species composition; larger values indicate greater turnover between sites. Gamma should be at least as large as alpha since it pools all sites.

name: Net Reproductive Rate (R0, Two Age Classes)
description: Calculates the net reproductive rate (R0), the average number of offspring produced by an individual over its lifetime, by summing the product of age-specific survivorship and fecundity across age classes from a life table. R0 > 1 indicates a growing population, R0 = 1 a stable population, and R0 < 1 a declining population.
notes: This simplified two-age-class version assumes discrete, non-overlapping reproductive events at ages 1 and 2 and constant survivorship/fecundity values across individuals; real life tables often include more age classes.

name: BOD Exerted after t Days
description: Gives the oxygen consumed by microbes in t days (BOD_t) from the ultimate BOD with first-order kinetics.
notes: BOD₅ is typically about two thirds of the ultimate BOD.

name: Sedimentation Tank Removal Fraction
description: Gives the fraction of particles of a given settling velocity removed by an ideal settling tank: their speed over the overflow rate Q/A (Hazen 1904).
notes: Depth does not matter in the ideal tank — surface area does.

name: Indoor CO₂ at Steady State
description: Gives the steady CO₂ level in a ventilated room from occupancy and outdoor-air supply — a proxy for ventilation adequacy.
notes: Below about 1000 ppm is generally considered well ventilated.
